summary: This memo reports measurements of round-trip times in the Internet and suggests improvements to how TCP computes its retransmission timeout. It serves as both a status report on the Internet and advice to TCP implementers.

plainLanguage.summary:
This memo reports two sets of measurements taken on the Internet in late 1983, and turns them into advice for people writing TCP.

The advice is about the retransmission timeout: how long TCP should wait before deciding that a packet was lost. The measurements showed that the rule in the specification reacted too slowly when the network suddenly got slower, and that the fix is to react faster to a rise in delay than to a fall.

questions: how does tcp choose retransmission timeout
how does tcp choose the retransmission timeout
does packet length affect network delay
subtitle: 1983 round-trip measurements across the Internet, and a tweak to TCP's retransmission timeout.

tldr.problem: TCP has to decide how long to wait before sending a segment again, and the rule in the specification had never been tested against real long and lossy paths.
tldr.mechanism: Mills measured round-trip times to hosts around the world with the early ping program, then replayed the measurements through a simulation of the timeout algorithm to see how it behaved.
tldr.outcome: The simulation showed the algorithm reacting too slowly to a sudden delay spike, which causes unnecessary retransmissions. The fix is to weight a rising delay sample more heavily than a falling one.

today: RFC 889 is an Informational document from December 1983 and has not been obsoleted. Its measurements describe the Internet of that time, with ARPANET, MILNET, MINET, SATNET and TELENET links and satellite hops of the kind that no longer carry ordinary traffic.

sections.title: The Experiments and the Measurement Host
sections.content:
The memorandum describes two series of experiments designed to explore the transmission characteristics of the Internet system. One series was designed to determine the network delays with respect to packet length, and the other to assess the effectiveness of the TCP retransmission-timeout algorithm specified in the standards documents. Both sets of experiments were conducted during the October to November 1983 time frame and used many hosts distributed throughout the Internet system.

The objectives were first to accumulate experimental data on actual network paths that could be used as a benchmark of Internet system performance, and second to apply these data to refine individual TCP implementations and improve their performance.

The experiments were done using a specially instrumented measurement host called a Fuzzball, which consists of an LSI-11 running IP and TCP and various application-layer protocols including Telnet, FTP and SMTP mail. Among the measurement packages is the original PING program, used over the last six years for numerous tests and measurements of the Internet system and its client nets. It can send various kinds of probe packets, including ICMP Echo messages, process the reply, and record elapsed times and other information in a data file, as well as produce real-time snapshot histograms and traces.

Following an experiment run, the data were reduced by another set of programs and plotted on a Peritek bit-map display with a colour monitor. The plots were found invaluable in identifying and understanding the causes of network glitches and other phenomena. The Fuzzballs and their local-net architecture, called DCN, had about two-dozen clones scattered worldwide, including one at the Linkabit Corporation offices in McLean, Virginia and another at the Norwegian Telecommunications Administration near Oslo. The remote test hosts were selected to represent canonical paths and were scattered all over the world, on the ARPANET, MILNET, MINET, SATNET, TELENET and numerous local nets reachable via these long-haul nets. Data were included for three different paths from the ARPANET-based measurement host to London hosts, two via different satellite links and one via an undersea cable.
sections.plainLanguage: The instrument was the ancestor of the modern ping command, and the machine it ran on was a small computer with an LSI processor wired into the network in the old packet-switched days.

sections.title: Packet Length Versus Delay
sections.content:
This set of experiments was designed to determine whether delays across the Internet are significantly influenced by packet length. In cases where the intrinsic propagation delays are high relative to the time to transmit an individual packet, one would expect that delays would not be strongly affected by packet length. That is the case with satellite nets, including SATNET and WIDEBAND, and also with terrestrial nets where the degree of traffic aggregation is high. Where the intrinsic propagation delays are low and the measured traffic represents the bulk of the traffic on the path, quite the opposite would be expected.

There were two sets of experiments, one based at DCN1 and the other at NTA. All used ICMP Echo and Reply messages with embedded timestamps. A cycle consisted of sending an ICMP Echo message of specified length, waiting for the corresponding Reply to come back and recording the elapsed time, normalized to one-way delay. An experiment run consisted of 512 of these volleys.

The length of each ICMP message was determined by a random-number generator uniformly distributed between zero and 256. Lengths below 40 were rounded up to 40, which is the minimum datagram size for an ICMP message containing timestamps and also happens to be the minimum TCP segment size. The maximum length was chosen to avoid complications due to fragmentation and reassembly, since ICMP messages are not ordinarily fragmented or reassembled by the gateways.

The data were first plotted as a scatter diagram. For all paths involving the ARPANET this immediately revealed two distinct characteristics, one for short single-packet messages of less than 126 octets and another for long multi-packet messages. The data clearly show a strong correlation between delay and length, with the longest packets showing delays two to three times the shortest. On paths via ARPANET clones the delay characteristic shows a stronger correlation with length for single-packet messages than for multi-packet messages, which is consistent with a design that favours low delays for short messages and high throughput for longer ones.

Most of the runs were made during off-peak hours, and in the few cases where runs were made for a host during both on-peak and off-peak hours the comparison shows a greater dependency on packet length than on traffic shift. TCP implementors should be advised that some dependency on packet length may have to be built into the retransmission-timeout estimation algorithm to insure good performance over lossy nets like SATNET, and that some Internet paths may require stupendous timeout intervals ranging to many seconds for the net alone, not to mention additional delays in host-system queues.
sections.plainLanguage: A bigger message takes longer to arrive. The surprise is how much longer: the biggest packets took two or three times as long as the smallest ones on the same path.

sections.title: The Retransmission-Timeout Algorithm
sections.content:
One of the basic features of TCP which allow it to be used on paths spanning many nets of widely varying delay and packet-loss characteristics is the retransmission-timeout algorithm, sometimes known as the RSRE algorithm for the original designers. The algorithm operates by recording the time and initial sequence number when a segment is transmitted, then computing the elapsed time for that sequence number to be acknowledged. There are various degrees of sophistication in the implementation, ranging from allowing only one such computation to be in progress at a time to allowing one for each segment outstanding at a time on the connection.

The algorithm is basically an estimation process. It maintains an estimate of the current round-trip delay time and updates it as new delay samples are computed. It smooths these samples and then establishes a timeout, which if exceeded causes a retransmission. The selection of the parameters of this algorithm is vitally important in order to provide effective data transmission and avoid abuse of the Internet system by excessive retransmissions.

The specified algorithm, really a first-order linear recursive filter, is characterized by two parameters, a weighting factor F and a threshold factor G. For each measured delay sample R the delay estimator E is updated as E = F*E + (1 - F)*R. Then, if an interval equal to G*E expires after transmitting a packet, the packet is retransmitted. The current TCP specification suggests values in the range 0.8 to 0.9 for F and 1.5 to 2.0 for G. These values have been believed reasonable up to now over ARPANET and SATNET paths.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP keeps a running estimate of how long the trip takes, and gives up and resends once the wait exceeds a multiple of that estimate. The memo asks whether the way that estimate is updated is right.

sections.title: What the Simulation Showed
sections.content:
The experiment data base was constructed of well over a hundred runs using ICMP Echo and Reply messages bounced off hosts scattered all over the world. Most runs consisted of 512 echo/reply cycles lasting from several seconds to twenty minutes or so; other runs designed to detect network glitches lasted several hours. The object was to simulate the packet delay distribution seen by TCP over the paths measured. Only the network delay is of interest, not the queueing delays within the hosts themselves, which can be considerable, and only a single packet was allowed in flight so that the stress on the network itself was minimal.

Each of the 512 data points collected during a run was plotted, with the time since the start of the experiment on one axis and the measured delay on the other, and then the simulated retransmission-timeout algorithm was run on these data and its computed timeout plotted in the same way. The display immediately reveals how the algorithm behaves in the face of varying traffic loads, network glitches, lost packets and superfluous retransmissions.

It is immediately obvious from the display that the delay distribution is more or less Poisson-distributed about a relatively narrow range, with important exceptions. The exceptions are characterized by occasional spasms where one or more packets can be delayed many times the typical value. What commonly happens is that the algorithm, when confronted with a short burst of long-delay packets after a relatively long interval of well-mannered behavior, takes much too long to adapt to the spasm. That invites many superfluous retransmissions and leads to congestion.

The incidence of long-delay bursts, or glitches, varied widely. Some runs were glitch-free, but most had at least one glitch in 512 echo/reply volleys. Glitches did not seem to correlate well with increases in baseline delay, which occurs as the result of traffic surges, nor did they correlate well with instances of packet loss. No particular periodicity was noticed, such as might be expected with regular pinging, though the data were not processed specially for that.

One particularly interesting experiment involved the FOE host, which is located in London and reached via a 14.4 Kbps undersea cable and statistical multiplexor. The multiplexor introduces a moderate mean delay, but with an extremely large delay dispersion. The specified retransmission-timeout algorithm had a hard time with this circuit, as might be expected, but with the improvements described below TCP performance was acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the time the trip takes about the same. Now and then it jumps, and the timeout rule takes far too long to notice, so TCP resends packets that were never lost. That is what clogs the network.

sections.title: The Proposed Improvement
sections.content:
The change proposed is a simple one that made a worthwhile difference in efficiency: use two values of F, one when the sample R is below the current estimate E and the other when R is at or above it, with F1 greater than F2. The effect is to make the algorithm more responsive to upward-going trends in delay and less responsive to downward-going trends.

After a number of trials the conclusion was that values of F1 = 15/16 and F2 = 3/4, with G = 2, gave the best all-around performance. The results on some paths, FOE, ISID and ISIA, were better by some ten percent in efficiency compared with the values then used in typical implementations, where F = 7/8 and G = 2. The results on most paths were better by five percent, while on a couple, FACC and UCL, the results were worse by a few percent.

There was no clear-cut gain in fiddling with G. The value G = 2 seemed to represent the best overall compromise. Increasing G makes superfluous retransmissions less likely, but increases the total delay when packets are lost. Increasing F2 too much tends to cause overshoot in the case of network glitches and leads to the same result.

Readers familiar with signal-detection theory will recognize the suggestion as analogous to an ordinary peak-detector circuit. F1 represents the discharge time-constant, F2 the charge time-constant, and G a squelch threshold as used in voice-operated switches.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix is to make the estimate rise quickly and fall slowly, so a sudden slowdown is noticed at once but a quick return to normal is not mistaken for the new normal.

items.title: F1, used when the sample is high
items.text: 15/16. A delay sample above the current estimate pulls the estimate up hard.

items.title: F2, used when the sample is low
items.text: 3/4. A delay sample below the current estimate pulls it down gently.

items.title: G, the threshold factor
items.text: 2. The packet is retransmitted when twice the estimate expires.

items.text: F = 7/8 and G = 2, which the new values improved on by five to ten percent of efficiency on most paths.
